newsitem.title: UK: Labour inherits healthy UK economy, tough decisions.
newsitem.headline: Labour inherits healthy UK economy, tough decisions.

text.p: Britain's new Labour government on Friday inherited an economy that is fundamentally healthy but it faces some tough policy decisions, possibly within days of taking office.

Defeated Prime Minister John Major spoke the truth when, announcing his resignation as Conservative party leader outside 10, Downing Street, he said: "The economy is booming, interest rates are low, inflation is low and unemployment is falling."
But many economists believe the country may be at a critical turning point.
The Bank of England says the inflation warning lights have been at red since late last year and has been pressing for interest rates to be raised from the present 6.0 percent.
New finance minister Gordon Brown is due to hear Bank Governor Eddie George's views in person at their first scheduled monetary policy meeting next Wednesday.

"Labour inherits an economy that is in serious danger of overheating this year and next year unless action is taken soon to curb economic growth," said David Walton, director of UK economic research at Goldman Sachs.
"Although the appreciation in sterling will hit the manufacturing and external sectors, interest rates still seem too low to curb the excessive buoyancy in consumer demand."

The problem with raising interest rates is that it could make life even more difficult for British industry, which is already struggling to sell its goods abroad because of a surge in the value of the pound since last summer.

Some economists therefore argue that a fiscal tightening -- either raising taxes or cutting public spending -- would be a more appropriate method of cooling the economy down without putting upward pressure on the pound.

"What the UK really needs is a windfall tax on households, not on the corporate sector," economists Glenn Davies and Andrew Smith of Credit Lyonnais wrote in an election commentary. They were referring to Labour's only concrete tax-raising pledge -- to levy a once-off "windfall tax" on the profits of privatised utility companies and use the money to take 250,000 young people off the unemployment register.

Labour has tied its hands to some extent on personal taxation by ruling out any increase in income tax rates. It has also pledged to live within tough spending limits laid down by the Conservatives for the next two years.
"There is still considerable scope for tax-raising measures," the Credit Lyonnais economists wrote.
For example, Labour could abolish tax relief on mortgage interest payments -- a significant move in a nation of home-owners -- and limit personal tax allowances.
The first moves on taxes could be announced in a mini-budget, which Brown has promised to introduce within two months.
The new Chancellor of the Exchequer is certain to tread carefully, however, as he is anxious to assure financial markets that Labour will be prudent in managing the economy.
The City of London, which long since succumbed to a "charm offensive" by Brown and new Prime Minister Tony Blair, took the landslide election victory in its stride on Friday.
London shares closed at a record high, partly inspired by a bullish Wall Street, as traders welcomed the certainty provided by a clear Labour win.
The pound recovered early losses and ended the day in buoyant mood, close to pre-election levels.

Richard Jeffrey, group economist at Charterhouse, said the British economic scene had changed dramatically under 18 years of Conservative government. Once the "sick man" of Europe, Britain was now at the top of the economic growth league.
"Looking ahead, the greatest challenge the new government faces is the preservation of a free-market environment in the face of the threat of ever-greater interference from the EU," he said.
